In this work, the ASL coating thickness was minimized and the slurry effects on coating quality were evaluated on doctor blade coatings, as well as the rheological properties of all three slurries, which contribute to a stable coating processibility window in slot-die coating. Highlights of the major progress include: • Successfully developed slurry formulation for slot-die coating • Fabricated both defect-free AFL and GDC with a very thin thickness (>5 m/min) • Fabricated thick ASL via slot-die coating (>5 m/min) In this quarter, we focused on evaluating the rheological properties of the ASL, AFL and GDC slurries with various solid contents, which will help predict the coating window. Slurry Formulation: Slurries of the AFL, ASL and GDC were prepared according to the formulations provided by Redox. Each formulation was prepared and tested with solid loadings of: 70 wt%, 65 wt%, 60 wt% and 55 wt%, a reasonable composition of binder, plasticizer, and dispersing agents. The slurries were prepared in a 2- step addition and 2 overnight mixing steps using a ball mill. Each mixing step was kept the same between slurries. Originally, slurries with a 75% solids content were targeted, however, only the ASL resulted in a homogeneous mixture, therefore further dilution and mixing was carried out to reach 70% solids for all three of the slurries, followed by coating each sample onto Mylar using the doctor blade method, and rheological evaluation of each slurry, as well as microscopy evaluation of the quality of the final, dried coatings. Rheology Study: 6 To evaluate the rheological behavior for the slurries at various levels of solid loading, a test method (described below) was used in a concentric cylinder rheometer (Discovery HR-3, TA Instruments) operated by TRIOS software. The instrument was calibrated, with the test cup equilibrated to 25 °C prior to transferring each of the prepared slurry samples, volumetrically into the test cup. Experimental Procedure: Step 1. Pre-shear of 5 s-1 applied for 60 s. – Provides consistent shear history between samples to reduce hysteresis effects. Step 2. Flow Ramp logarithmic ramp between 5 to 3500 s-1 over 5 min. – Measures stress, providing the samples viscosity as a function of shear rate. Step 3. Oscillation Time Sweep angular frequency (ω) of 100 rad·s -1 and oscillation strain (g) of 0.1% for 15 min. – Rebuilds the fluid’s bridging flocculation network structure which is disrupted at high shear rates. Step 4. Amplitude Sweep ω = 100 rad·s-1, between g = 0.01-10% – Characterizes strength of network structure by measuring the dependency of G’ and G’’ on strain. Step 5. Oscillation Time Sweep angular frequency (ω) of 100 rad·s -1 and oscillation strain g of 0.1% for 5 min. – Shorter rebuild time required for amplitude sweep (less destructive than the flow ramp test).
